stem: How many poliovirus serotypes are there, and does immunity to one protect against the others?

options.label: A
options.text: One serotype; immunity to it protects against all strains
options.misconception: Assumes poliovirus, like measles virus, is antigenically uniform so one infection protects against all.
options.explanation: Poliovirus is not a single serotype; CDC lists types 1, 2 and 3, so immunity to one strain cannot cover all polio.

options.label: B
options.text: Two serotypes; immunity to one protects against the other
options.misconception: Misremembers the serotype count and assumes cross-protection between them.
options.explanation: Two is the wrong count; CDC lists three poliovirus serotypes, and immunity to one does not protect against the others.

options.label: C
options.text: Three serotypes; immunity to one protects against all three
options.misconception: Knows the count but assumes antibodies to one serotype neutralize the other two.
options.explanation: The count is right but the cross-protection is wrong: immunity to one poliovirus serotype gives no significant immunity to the others.

options.label: D
options.text: Four serotypes; immunity to one gives little cross-protection
options.misconception: Transfers the four-serotype pattern of dengue virus onto poliovirus.
options.explanation: Dengue virus, not poliovirus, has four serotypes, and cross-protection between them is only short-lived; poliovirus has three serotypes.

options.label: E
options.text: Three serotypes; immunity to one gives little cross-protection
options.misconception: None — three serotypes with no significant cross-immunity.
options.explanation: CDC lists three poliovirus serotypes (types 1, 2 and 3) and states that immunity to one does not produce significant immunity to the others.

context: Learning objective: Poliovirus has three serotypes (types 1, 2 and 3), and immunity to one gives no significant immunity to the others.
